title: SprayClear
question: How does a spray bottle work?
hook: One squeeze of your finger makes about 4.6 bar, shuts one tiny ball, opens another and tears a millilitre of water into drops thinner than a hair. Pull the trigger of a spray bottle in slow motion and watch it happen.

explainer.title: A tiny hand pump on a bottle
explainer.text: A trigger sprayer screws onto a bottle and needs no gas or battery. A lever drives a piston in a small cylinder, a spring brings it back, and two ball valves make the flow go one way.

explainer.title: Squeeze, then let go
explainer.text: Squeezing with 20 N on a 3 to 1 lever makes about 4.6 bar, which shuts the inlet ball and opens the outlet. Letting go lowers the cylinder's pressure, and the air on the bottle's liquid pushes about 1 mL up the tube. A dry pump takes a few pulls to prime.

explainer.title: From a jet to a mist
explainer.text: Pressure gives up to 30 m/s at the hole. A swirl chamber spins the liquid into a hollow cone. The thin sheet tears into threads, and surface tension pinches them into drops about 60 microns across in our model.

explainer.title: How far and how fine
explainer.text: Drag brakes small drops within centimetres, and they can evaporate in seconds, while 1 mm drops from the stream setting fly over 4 metres. Thick oils and gels are too sluggish to mist.

explainer.title: The cousins
explainer.text: A perfume bulb and an airbrush really use suction, from fast air. An aerosol can stores its pressure in a propellant. A pump-up knapsack stores it in air you pump by hand.

explainer.title: Use it safely
explainer.text: A disinfectant needs its label's contact time, wet on the surface. Never mix cleaning products: some combinations give off toxic gas. Label every refill, keep sprays from eyes and children, and follow pesticide labels.

concepts.def: A pump that moves a fixed amount of liquid each stroke by squeezing a closed space.
A one-way gate, here a small ball that flow lifts off its seat in one direction and shuts in the other.
Replacing the air in a pump and tube with liquid so it can build pressure.
A tiny room behind the nozzle hole where side-entering liquid spins, so it leaves as a hollow cone.
The pull between molecules at a liquid's surface that makes it act like a stretched skin.
A ratio of how hard moving liquid pushes against how strongly surface tension holds it together.
Why a thread of liquid pinches into beads: spheres have less surface.
How long a disinfectant must stay wet on a surface for the label's claim to hold.
The gas in an aerosol can that stores the pressure and pushes the product out.
